tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section compares libjson directly with encoding/json (json.Unmarshal into `any`), using public code: BenchmarkLibJson_* and BenchmarkEncodingJson_* in json_test.go, and benchmarks/bench.sh + gen.py (hyperfine on cmd/lj.go). The go test output names the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3700X), but no Go toolchain version is stated (go.mod gives only a minimum, go 1.26.4), so by the orchestrator's Go rule (goccy/go-json, constmap retier) this is C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem with default Go build flags; Go toolchain version not stated (go.mod declares only a minimum, go 1.26.4). File benchmarks: go build + hyperfine (--warmup 1 --runs 10).
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X 8-Core Processor, linux/amd64 (stated in the go test output; the hyperfine file benchmark does not restate hardware)
corrections.caveats: Very small project (5 stars, single author). The 'Naive'/'Escaped'/'Hard' inputs are self-defined strings repeated inside json_test.go, not a standard external corpus. No Go toolchain version is stated. libjson mutates its input buffer for zero-copy parsing, while encoding/json unmarshals into `any` without that trade-off. The hyperfine file benchmark does not restate the machine.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup (1.94x/2.29x/2.43x ns/op, 2.10x-3.14x fewer allocs, 1.69x-1.81x on 1MB-100MB files) matches the README. The recorded benchmark_url used /blob/main/, which returns 404; the default branch is master. Metadata checks out: MIT, 5 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-06-06 (active).

tier_reason: The page and docs/bench-report.md compare metal-json directly with vendored C++ simdjson v4.6.4 (DOM tape API). The code is public (bench/benches/compare.rs, bench/src/lib.rs, bench/cpp/shim.cpp, bench/build.rs, driven by `cargo run -p xtask -- bench-report`), and the report gives the CPU (Apple M5 Max), rustc 1.95.0, the Metal toolchain version and the baseline flags (-O3, C++17, NDEBUG, -mcpu=native). But the C++ compiler that built the simdjson baseline is never named or versioned (only 'cc -O3', meaning the Rust cc crate's system default). By the same rule as simdxml (wave 4) and the Go toolchain retier, that is C, one fact short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On twitter-shaped documents, 1.34x-2.71x faster than C++ simdjson from 8 MiB to 512 MiB (1.34x at 8 MiB, 1.81x at 16 MiB, 2.28x at 64 MiB, 2.06x/2.19x/2.71x at 100/256/512 MiB; 7.51 vs 2.77 GB/s at 512 MiB). On number-dense canada.json it is 1.42x faster at 2.1 MiB. It loses below the ~4.3 MiB twitter crossover: 0.96x at 4 MiB, 0.33x at 1 MiB, 0.12x (simdjson ~8x faster) at 0.6 MiB, and 0.44x on citm_catalog (1.6 MiB).
corrections.workload: Parse-to-tape plus an identical stats walk (node count, unescaped string bytes, XOR of number payloads) inside the timed region, for both metal-json (Metal GPU kernels) and C++ simdjson's DOM tape API. The inputs are canonical twitter/citm_catalog/canada from simdjson-data plus deterministic twitter-template expansions from 1 MiB to 512 MiB. An untimed check asserts bit-identical stats before timing.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: simdjson v4.6.4 amalgamation built through the Rust cc crate with -O3 -std=c++17 -DNDEBUG and -mcpu=native on aarch64 (bench/build.rs). The C++ compiler and its version are not stated. metal-json: rustc 1.95.0 and Apple Metal toolchain 32023.883 (per bench-report.md). Criterion medians.
corrections.caveats: Single machine and single vendor (one Apple M5 Max; the library runs only on Apple Silicon Metal). All rows of 1 MiB and above are expansions of the twitter template. canada and citm_catalog were measured only at their 1.6-2.1 MiB canonical sizes, so the 100-512 MiB wins cover twitter-shaped data only. The crossover (~4.3 MiB) depends on document shape and machine: canada already wins at 2.1 MiB, while citm_catalog still favors simdjson at 1.6 MiB. The timed work is a full DOM parse to tape plus a shallow stats walk on both sides. simdjson On-Demand was deliberately not compared. The C++ compiler version for the simdjson build is not stated. The project is young and small: first commit 2026-06-11, the benchmark report dated 2026-06-12, 54 commits, 18 stars. The README says 'MIT OR Apache-2.0', but the LICENSE file and Cargo.toml say MIT only.

notes: Every number in the record matches the page and bench-report.md exactly (0.12x at 0.6 MiB, 1.34x at 8 MiB, 2.06x-2.71x at 100-512 MiB, ~4.3 MiB crossover, M5 Max/128 GiB/macOS 26.5.1, simdjson v4.6.4 -O3 -mcpu=native). The record's caveats had two errors: 'stage-1/tape build only' is wrong, since both sides do a full DOM parse to tape plus a stats walk, and 'first commits this month' is wrong, since the first commit is 2026-06-11. The downgrade rests only on the unnamed C++ compiler for the baseline. If the orchestrator accepts the cc crate's system default (Apple clang, version unknown) as enough, this could stay A. Metadata checks out: MIT, 18 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-21 (active).

tier_reason: The README Performance tables compare zenjson directly with RapidJSON (and simdjson and nlohmann/json) on the nativejson-benchmark files. The code is public: benchmark/jsonbenchmark.cpp (one TARGET macro per library, clock() over N=1000) and benchmark/jsonbenchmark.vcxproj (toolset v141; Release|x64 = MaxSpeed /O2, IntrinsicFunctions, WholeProgramOptimization, NDEBUG). The README states the compiler (Visual Studio 2017, 64-bit), the per-library flags (RAPIDJSON_SSE2/ParseInsitu, simdjson /std:c++17) and the CPU (i7-7700K), so it meets A. It is borderline: the README never says 'Release' explicitly (the committed project file supplies it), and the third-party library versions are neither stated nor vendored.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Parsing (derived from page data): 1.81x-3.57x faster than RapidJSON (twitter.json 2034.7 vs 570.3 MB/s = 3.57x; canada.json 3.048 vs 5.509 ms = 1.81x; citm_catalog.json 0.715 vs 1.869 ms = 2.61x). 13.8x-26.7x faster than nlohmann/json. Slightly slower than simdjson on twitter and citm (by 1-3%), and simdjson is 1.46x faster on canada. Stringifying (derived from page data): 2.64x-4.25x faster than RapidJSON (0.712 vs 1.877 ms, 8.723 vs 24.125 ms, 0.777 vs 3.299 ms) and 7.8x-15.3x faster than nlohmann/json.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (MSVC toolset v141), 64-bit. The committed benchmark/jsonbenchmark.vcxproj Release|x64 uses MaxSpeed (/O2), IntrinsicFunctions (/Oi), WholeProgramOptimization and NDEBUG. RapidJSON uses RAPIDJSON_SSE2 and ParseInsitu. simdjson is compiled with /std:c++17 and allocate_capacity pre-allocation. The others use default settings.
corrections.caveats: No commits since 2019-09-16 (abandoned) and only 8 stars. The benchmark ran on a single 2017-era Windows/MSVC machine, with no Linux/GCC/Clang numbers. Library versions are not stated, and the RapidJSON/simdjson/nlohmann headers are not in the repo; the simdjson row uses the 2019 ParsedJson/json_parse API. In the stringify loop, RapidJSON's StringBuffer and PrettyWriter are never cleared between the 1000 iterations, so its stringify time includes appending and regrowing an ever-larger buffer; zenjson overwrites a fixed 4 MB buffer. zenjson and RapidJSON pretty-print, while nlohmann's dump() is compact. zenjson parses in situ, mutating the input. The README does not say Release explicitly; the Release|x64 settings come from the committed .vcxproj.

notes: Every raw number in the record's examples appears in the README, but none of the ratios is on the page, and the paraphrased ranges were wrong. The parse lower bound was overstated ('~2x'; canada.json is really 1.81x). The stringify ranges were understated (4.25x vs RapidJSON and 15.3x vs nlohmann on citm_catalog). Tier A is kept, so this is a claim-only downgrade. The stringify comparison against RapidJSON is biased by a harness flaw (the output buffer is never cleared), so the orchestrator should lead with the parse numbers. Metadata checks out: MIT, 8 stars, not a fork, last commit 2019-09-16.
